title: Genesis
subtitle: From zero to a full-stack app in 33 days, all through direct commits
narrative:
Before there were pull requests, before there was a PR workflow, there was a founder and an AI pair-programming partner building as fast as they could. In 33 days and 29 direct-to-main commits, Kindred Reels went from an empty repository to a fully functional full-stack application with cloud infrastructure.

The journey started on October 19 with a LICENSE file and a Vite/Express skeleton. Three weeks of intense building followed: a working photo upload and voice recording app with SQLite (Nov 9), migration to DynamoDB and S3 for cloud-native storage (Nov 10), AWS Lambda deployment with GitHub Actions CI/CD (Nov 11), Google OAuth authentication via Cognito (Nov 11), per-user project authorization (Nov 15), a Python video generation pipeline with Ken Burns effects (Nov 19), cloud video processing through SQS and Lambda containers (Nov 19), and finally the migration to EC2 Spot instances when Lambda's 15-minute timeout proved insufficient (Nov 21).

Every commit was pushed directly to main — no branches, no reviews, just rapid iteration. The commit messages were informal and raw: 'whole mess of claude contributions..', 'fixed frontend action hopefully', 'lots of github action secrets for oauth.' This was the bootstrapping era, where speed mattered more than process. By November 21, the PR workflow would be adopted, but the architectural foundations laid in this phase — the monorepo structure, DynamoDB single-table design, S3 media storage, Lambda API, EC2 video processing — would persist throughout the project's evolution.

title: The First Reel, and Sadie Joins
subtitle: The core loop takes shape, memories become the heart of the product, and a second person starts committing
narrative:
With the PR workflow adopted, a solo founder and an AI coding assistant built the skeleton of an entirely new kind of family product — and then discovered its true shape. The very first PR introduced shareable contribution links, the defining interaction of the platform, where family members could record voice memories for photos without creating an account. Within a week the codebase had beat-synced video generation, multi-method authentication through AWS Cognito, an admin panel, GPU-accelerated processing on EC2, and AWS Rekognition face detection guiding cinematic Ken Burns camera movements. The project was renamed from 'Loomed Memories' to 'Kindred Reels' during this sprint, and the backend, frontend, and video pipeline were all functional from the start — shipped as a cohesive system rather than built incrementally.

The biggest conceptual breakthrough came next: the evolution from 'photo groups' to 'Memories' — the realization that the atomic unit of the product wasn't a photo or a recording, but a memory: a voice narration attached to one to five photos that becomes a segment in the final video. This shift touched nearly every layer of the system and took several PRs to fully realize. Alongside it, the mobile experience was overhauled to make contribution feel natural on a phone: compact recording UI, volume visualization, auto-playing slideshow previews, and a focused recording mode.

The production deployment pipeline shipped with email and SMS invitations, making the platform usable by real families for the first time. The Video Builder emerged as a drag-and-drop timeline editor with sections, the color scheme was standardized across the UI with CSS custom properties, and a comprehensive frontend test suite of 1,742 tests was generated in a single AI-assisted session. Direct-to-main commits continued for quick operational work — a refreshed landing page, EC2 and CI/CD docs, Linux font fixes, 4K rendering, and a batch of production fixes. By December 10, Kindred Reels had found its voice, both literally and conceptually.

Then, on December 2, someone else started committing. Sadie Bilenkin, Dimitri's daughter and a software engineer, began writing unit tests for the backend's project handler, with small helpers that stand in for the database so the tests run on their own. Like Dimitri she worked mostly through Claude Code, but she also wrote code by hand here and there, especially when she was finding her way into a new area. Her pull request merged on December 8: the first from anyone but Dimitri. It was 417 lines in a codebase of about 70,000, and it changed what Kindred Reels was. From here on, two people were building it.
sadieNote: Sadie's first commit landed on December 2 and her first pull request, #43, merged on December 8: unit tests for creating, reading and deleting projects, the backend's first handler tests. Until then every line had come from Dimitri working with Claude Code. It is the moment the project got a second engineer, and a second pair of eyes checking that the code did what it claimed.

title: The Intelligence Layer
subtitle: AI transforms curation, and the video output turns cinematic
narrative:
This phase marked the pivot from a manual curation tool to an AI-powered storytelling platform whose output looked genuinely professional. The AI Producer evolved through three generations: v1 prototyped with Gemini for basic photo analysis, v2 integrated Rekognition face clustering with the Gemini Files API for richer understanding, and later refinements added pre-upload optimization and face deduplication. The music system gained multi-track support with automatic audio ducking — background music that gracefully dips when voice recordings play. The frontend underwent its own transformation with a major state management refactor from prop drilling to React Query and Zustand, establishing the architectural patterns for everything that followed.

A photo enhancement pipeline brought Google Cloud Storage, Gemini-powered quality analysis, and Cloud Run GPU restoration. The Timeline Contributor Flow launched, letting invited family members browse the entire project timeline rather than just their assigned photos, and Google Photos integration via the Picker API eliminated the friction of uploads. The CodeChronicle codebase analytics dashboard — the ancestor of this very project — was added to the main repo.

The new year opened with a laser focus on output quality. The AI Producer was refactored into a clean 4-stage workflow with extensively engineered Gemini prompts. HTML-based slides replaced static images for title screens, credits, and section dividers — rendered through Playwright into crisp, resolution-independent frames. Whisper AI transcription brought closed captions, with an editor for hosts to correct the AI's work. The timeline UX went through a six-stage polish sprint, the music system gained track metadata and a table-based admin library, and video rendering improvements delivered attribution slides, fade-to-black outros, and the first named theme: 'noir-elegant.' By mid-January, Kindred Reels could intelligently analyze, organize, and present family photo collections — and the videos it produced were the kind families would be proud to share.

Sadie's part of this chapter was the safety net under all that speed. In the first two weeks of January she brought her project tests up to date with a month of API changes, then wrote tests for most of the backend in six days: sign-in, the AI Producer, music, Google Photos, memories, invitations and five admin handlers. That one pull request was 12,175 lines, and test code grew from about 25,000 lines to about 36,000 over the chapter. In December her photo had gone up beside Dimitri's on a new About page, listed as Software Engineer.
sadieNote: Sadie's biggest contribution to the codebase came here. She updated her project tests for a month of API changes (#77), then tested most of the backend's handlers in six days: 12,175 lines across 21 files (#91). On December 20 the new About page introduced the team as two people, with her photo beside Dimitri's (#60).

title: Events, Scale & the Great Hardening
subtitle: Weddings and reunions, a professional curation experience, and a security-and-quality reckoning
narrative:
Kindred Reels had proven itself for tribute videos, but the product vision was broader: any gathering where photos and stories intersect. This phase introduced Event projects alongside the existing Tribute type, designed for weddings, parties, and reunions where multiple people contribute photos in real time. The Event Organizer flow was the centerpiece — an AI pipeline that analyzes hundreds of photos, detects temporal clusters, identifies key people, and generates a named-section timeline. Deferred Rekognition avoided expensive face detection at upload time, and the 28-template theme system launched, offering five aesthetic families all rendered through Playwright.

With the feature set largely complete, attention turned to making everything work beautifully at scale. The organization mode UX overhaul delivered a professional photo-curation experience with a full-screen lightbox, side-by-side comparison, and cluster visualization, while optimistic updates made photo replacement feel instant. A critical performance fix eliminated N+1 DynamoDB queries that had caused 13-second page loads, bringing them down to 1-2 seconds. The music system got a curated, mood-organized library with AI auto-selection, the project creation flow was unified across types, a public Technology page was added, and the repository migrated to the kindredreels organization on GitHub.

Meanwhile Sadie moved from unit tests to the browser. Her Playwright tests signed in like a real person and walked a project from creation to deletion, the first checks of the app the way people use it. She also fixed sideways phone photos in six lines, by applying the rotation the camera records when thumbnails are made.

Then came the reckoning, and Sadie led it. Before friends and family were invited, the project needed a security audit, and the brief was written for her. It opened with a known hole: guessing a project's id could open someone else's project. She fixed authorization on the API's routes and moved file access onto signed, expiring links. Dimitri finished the work on her branch: one shared ownership check on every project route, private storage behind CloudFront, 63 error responses that no longer leaked internal details, and database point-in-time recovery. Alongside it, the sharing track delivered public watch pages with share codes, QR codes and direct YouTube upload. The backend, frontend and Python pipeline each went through a five-phase hardening pass, and the test suite became a hard gate that blocks deploys. The result was a safer, better-tested product that people could share.
sadieNote: Sadie wrote the project's first browser tests with Playwright: the home page, signing in, and a project's whole life from creation to deletion (#106, #109). She fixed sideways phone photos (#117). And she led the security audit that opened the Great Hardening: route authorization and signed file links on her branch (#127), finished there with shared ownership checks and private storage (#128). That audit is why friends and family could be invited safely.

title: The Cutting Room
subtitle: Video clips arrive, and the platform learns to edit motion, cost, and color
narrative:
For its entire life, Kindred Reels had worked with still photos. This phase brought it into motion. Video clips arrived as a full pipeline: videos import from Google Photos or upload directly from a device into Google Cloud Storage, a Cloud Run video-processor service runs FFmpeg plus Gemini analysis to identify the best moments, and the EC2 renderer stitches chosen clips into the timeline with music ducking for footage carrying meaningful audio. The clip experience matured quickly — clip extraction was deferred to render time (echoing the defer-until-generation cost pattern used elsewhere), a unified ClipPlayer gained draggable in/out handles for boundary editing, post-credits sections and per-clip ducking joined the mix, and a stubborn class of clip audio sync drift was finally eliminated by embedding audio in segments and rebuilding the timeline from probed durations. Smart ducking learned to read a Gemini audioSignificance rating, letting concerts stay loud and wind noise stay quiet.

Underneath the features, the platform grew a cost consciousness. Per-project cost tracking instrumented every Gemini, Rekognition, Whisper, Cloud Run, and EC2 call, surfacing in the admin UI exactly what each project cost to produce. GCP environments were isolated so dev and prod stopped sharing infrastructure, admin dashboard performance was rescued with shared server-side caches, and a GCP cost exploration corrected Vertex pricing and shut off idle-CPU billing. The AI pipeline gained deterministic project classification and composable, category-aware architect prompts.

The surface got a serious polish, too. The Timeline detail view and Organization lightbox were consolidated into one metadata-rich UnifiedLightbox, cover-photo handling was unified with a picker in the generate modal, and 19 emoji icons gave way to clean SVGs. A comprehensive branded email system with seven transactional types shipped alongside a rewritten login page, YouTube API compliance disclosures landed, and — most visibly — a sweeping semantic token refactor migrated ~2,500 raw color classes into 27 CSS variables, unlocking a full light mode across 167 files. The cutting room was open, and the product had learned to edit not just video, but its own cost and color.

One piece of this chapter lives outside the repository. Sadie built the project's first real monitoring: a Grafana dashboard, running as its own small service on Google Cloud and reading the app's logs from AWS through a read-only account, so the platform could be watched in one place instead of log by log. It was set up separately from the main codebase, which is why no pull request here carries it.
sadieNote: Sadie built the Grafana dashboard that monitored the app's logs, the first time Kindred Reels had a place to watch how it was running. It ran as its own service on Google Cloud, fed by a read-only account on AWS, and was committed outside this repository, so it has no entry below. It was live by April 2026.

title: Timeline v2 & the Curation Engine
subtitle: A new editing surface and a deterministic, merit-scored curation pipeline
narrative:
After a quiet stretch, the project returned with two of its most ambitious efforts. The GCS buckets were consolidated into us-east4 — first by lifting bucket names onto stage-aware environment variables, then executing the region move as a pure data migration with no code changes. Then came the largest single PR in the project's history at nearly 24,000 lines: the Timeline-v2 drag-and-drop redesign. It reimagined timeline editing as a single merged surface with live within-section rearrange, cursor-positional drops, cross-section drag with auto-expand and auto-scroll, drag-to-remove, multi-select, and multi-drag with a stacked overlay and floating action bar — the kind of direct-manipulation editing that makes a tool feel professional.

Beneath the new surface, the intelligence that decides what goes into a video was substantially rebuilt. Deterministic temporal segmentation took over from the Gemini architect for chronological projects, with a balanced dynamic-programming partitioner fixing pathological section splits, demoting the AI to a fallback role. The curation overhaul introduced a content-value gate that assigns every photo a contentRole and hard-excludes functional captures, a four-dimension highlightMerit score that lets the curator rank on quality, an index-based response contract, and a merit floor where per-section targets are an aim rather than a quota — any theme may keep nothing if everything in it is weak. Cover-photo selection became curator-nominated and image-aware. Secrets were hardened into AWS Secrets Manager, and a seven-phase documentation overhaul rebuilt the reference docs against live infrastructure, running eleven adversarial checkers against 600 claims and shrinking the always-loaded doc context from ~1,970 lines to 46. The photo library was flattened to individual tiles, cluster dedup was enforced, and a warm-voice copy pass stripped the last robotic language from the product's face.

title: Ready for Company
subtitle: Measure everything, make feedback easy, look the part, and listen to friends and family
narrative:
July turned a working product into one that could have guests. Correctness came first: photo times were read with their real time zones, so sections stopped splitting in strange places, and a zero-warning lint pass cleaned up 1,728 warnings and found a real bug on the way. Admin pages that read the whole database were moved onto a shared index, and a scheduled sweep started catching videos stuck in processing.

Then the product turned outward. The landing page got its signature animation, photos piling into a little curation machine and coming out as a film strip. A feedback button and an admin triage page made it easy to say what went wrong, and failures started offering to report themselves. A five-part instrumentation push recorded who uploaded what, counted share views, emailed the founder on failures and built a daily funnel. The public watch page learned to invite viewers to make their own. And, with Dimitri talking the choices through with Sadie, the whole app was repainted in a warm photo-album look, with a new mark called the Solid Weave and a light theme by default.

Early August brought the first feedback from friends and family, and the first surprises about cost: a June database bill traced to a browser tab polling an endpoint that read the whole table, and a dashboard poll that used 964,000 database reads in an hour. Both were fixed at the root. The chapter closed with plans and prices: four tiers, features gated by tier, upload caps, a pricing probe that shows real prices without taking any money, and a render progress bar fitted to real renders until it landed within 9%.
sadieNote: Sadie was Dimitri's sounding board for design throughout the year, and the warm retheme, the new Solid Weave mark and the landing page were the kind of decisions he talked through with her. That work does not show up as commits, but it shows up in how the product looks.

title: The First Strangers
subtitle: Payments built and switched off, people nobody invited, and the bugs only real use finds
narrative:
Payments were built and then deliberately switched off. Before taking anyone's money, the founder wanted to know whether people would pay, so the pricing probe kept running while Stripe sat ready behind a switch. A cost review in the same week found the AWS bill was about $8 a month, not the $150 that had been assumed, and budgets went up on both clouds.

In late August, strangers started arriving with no launch at all, and analytics credited ChatGPT for some of them. Real use found what testing had not. Contributor uploads failed on bad networks, so uploads learned to survive them, duplicates were caught, and add-photos links began to work for whole groups. Contributors could import from Google Photos. YouTube uploads were rebuilt to resume in chunks. A new user with 327 photos could never make a video until the render job moved to S3. A watched session with a tester named Joe produced a batch of fixes, and deleted projects turned out to leave public thumbnails behind, which a row of fixes closed.

The way of working firmed up alongside. The beta lived in a tracker of numbered buckets, updated in the same commit as the work. Merges had to pass tests first, a browser smoke suite ran against real stages, and releases deployed the renderer before the backend. CLAUDE.md gained two rules that say a lot about this partnership: "You wrote all of this code", so no bug is ever someone else's, and "Write plainly". The site was made readable for search engines and AI crawlers, shared links began showing the reel instead of a logo, and the funnel started measuring whether anyone actually watched. The chapter ends with six sessions of timeline-quality work, started by reviewing 23 strangers' timelines by hand: better picks, dates fixed at the root, clips judged like photos, and videos that open and end on purpose.

title: Protect the People Already Using It
subtitle: A security pass in tiers, the founder's keys off the hot path, and a film that ends well
narrative:
With strangers using the product, the parking lot was rebuilt as one list sorted by risk, and its first tier had a plain name: protect the people already using it. Tribute face matching started asking for consent. The privacy policy and terms were rewritten to describe the real product. Share links were limited to what their kind of link allows, accounts could no longer be taken over through a lookalike signup, users could delete their own account, and stored Google tokens were encrypted.

The founder's own keys came off the hot path. The renderer stopped deploying over SSH and port 22 closed. CI signed in to AWS and then Google Cloud with short-lived credentials instead of a stored key, the backend's cloud roles got a hard permissions ceiling, and video callbacks stopped trusting one shared password. Removing that password exposed deleted videos coming back as ghost records, and they now stay deleted. Tier 1 shipped to production as v0.1.32 on October 2.

Two quieter changes said a lot about the project. The working style was written down as four agent roles, recon, builder, reviewer and integrator, so every change is planned, built and checked by separate hands. And in the middle of the security work, the film learned to end well: instead of a still card in silence, videos now close on the Solid Weave mark drawing itself while the last song plays on. The landing page got a matching piece, The Loom, a short animated reel of how a video gets made.
sadieNote: The monitoring Sadie started grew up in this chapter. Her Grafana dashboard had been the project's first view of its own logs; on September 22 it was retired in the cleanup of old cloud services, and within days production had built-in alerts for being down, slow, backed up or crashing.

title: The Final Cut
subtitle: The film itself gets its craft, and the last gates before a public beta close
narrative:
The last stretch went back to the thing the product exists to make. One request for faster photos became a Photo pace setting, Relaxed, Normal or Fast, and making the paces fit the music meant rewriting beat timing, which revealed that cuts had never quite landed on the beat. Now they do. Photos got real camera moves, zooming in, pulling back or panning depending on the faces in them, then gentler zooms so portraits stop racing. Static that had crept into voice recordings was removed at the source.

The landing page was finished with three real sample films, including the 70th-birthday tribute Dimitri made for his parents, a public How it's built page, and a perfect accessibility score. The pre-launch security and capacity review was closed out, from account linking to email sending limits to the last whole-table reads. Rendering moved to Google Cloud Run Jobs, one job per video with the old EC2 box as a fallback, so a busy launch day cannot queue everyone behind one machine. Photos from 200-megapixel phones began to work, renders could be cancelled, and every email took on the app's warm colors.

The final pull request, on October 6, redesigned the title slides: twelve themes that look different from each other, photos cropped around faces, and titles that keep off people's faces. 353 days after an empty repository, Kindred Reels stood at about 258,000 lines and 250 pull requests, built by Dimitri through Claude Code without writing code directly, with Sadie's tests and security work under it, and ready for a public beta.
sadieNote: Sadie's name goes out with the product. The company page reads "Built by Dimitri Bilenkin and his daughter Sadie", and the launch post tells the story the same way: the tool the two of them built over the past year. The redesigned title themes and the finished landing page are the kind of design calls Dimitri bounced off her along the way.
